claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ge et al., 2018 and Bernassola et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Defects in genome maintenance increase the chance that various constituents of cellular pathways will experience alterations that favor tumor cell proliferation, survival, and metastasis.
claims.source: Changes in the maintenance of the genome, epigenome, transcriptome, and proteome occupy a central position because they increase the chance that various constituents of other cellular pathways will experience alterations that favor the acquisition of capabilities that permit the proliferation, survival, and metastasis of tumor cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Complex structural changes of the genome occur early in carcinogenesis, whereas point mutations occur in later disease phases.
claims.source: Recent studies on the chronology and genomic landscape of the events that drive carcinogenesis suggest that complex structural changes of the genome occur early, whereas point mutations occur in later disease phases (Maura et al., 2019; Voronina et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Maura et al., 2019 and Voronina et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The number of cancer driving mutations needed for the full development of cancer ranges from two to eight depending on cancer type.
claims.source: According to current estimates, the number of cancer driving mutations needed for the full development of cancer ranges from two-eight depending on cancer type (Vogelstein and Kinzler, 2015; Anandakrishnan et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Vogelstein and Kinzler, 2015 and Anandakrishnan et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Cancer genomes contain, on average, four to five driver mutations.
claims.source: A recent integrative analysis of 2658 whole-cancer genomes and their matching normal tissues across 38 tumor types revealed that, on average, cancer genomes contain four to five driver mutations (Campbell et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Campbell et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Mutations of genes that regulate apoptosis occur in the early phases of tumor progression.
claims.source: Although the temporal order of the mutations affecting genes of key pathways differs among cancer types, it appears that a common feature is that mutations of genes that regulate apoptosis occur in the early phases of tumor progression, whereas mutations of genes involved in invasion pathways occur only in the last stages of carcinogenesis (Gerstung et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gerstung et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Mutations of genes involved in invasion pathways occur only in the last stages of carcinogenesis.
claims.source: Although the temporal order of the mutations affecting genes of key pathways differs among cancer types, it appears that a common feature is that mutations of genes that regulate apoptosis occur in the early phases of tumor progression, whereas mutations of genes involved in invasion pathways occur only in the last stages of carcinogenesis (Gerstung et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gerstung et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Loss of apoptotic control is a critical step for initiating cancer because larger surviving cell populations have higher numbers of cells at risk of acquiring additional mutations.
claims.source: It has been suggested that the reason why the loss of apoptotic control is a critical step for initiating cancer is that the larger the surviving cell population, the higher the number of cells at risk of acquiring additional mutations.
claims.evidence: This is presented as a suggested explanation in the manuscript.

claims.claim: BRAF, KRAS, TP53, RB, and APC are key genes whose mutation is most likely to initiate carcinogenesis.
claims.source: Analyses of the mutation landscapes and evolutionary trajectories of various tumor tissues have identified BRAF, KRAS, TP53, RB, or APC as the key genes whose mutation is most likely to initiate carcinogenesis, permitting the cell to divide abnormally (Vogelstein and Kinzler, 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vogelstein and Kinzler, 2015.

claims.claim: TP53 mutation is the earliest tumorigenic driver event in ovarian cancers, present in nearly all cases.
claims.source: In the case of ovarian cancers, TP53 mutation is believed to be the earliest tumorigenic driver event, with presence in nearly all cases of ovarian cancer (Bashashati et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bashashati et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The vast majority of melanomas harbor TERT promoter mutations, indicating that these immortalizing mutations are selected at an early stage of neoplastic progression.
claims.source: Studies on the evolution of melanoma from precursor lesions have revealed that the vast majority of melanomas harbor TERT promoter mutations, indicating that these immortalizing mutations are selected at an unexpectedly early stage of neoplastic progression (Shain et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shain et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Early oncogenesis is characterized by mutations in a constrained set of driver genes.
claims.source: This study has shown that early oncogenesis is characterized by mutations in a constrained set of driver genes and that the driver mutations that most commonly occur in a given cancer also tend to occur the earliest (Gerstung et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gerstung et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Driver mutations that most commonly occur in a given cancer tend to occur the earliest.
claims.source: This study has shown that early oncogenesis is characterized by mutations in a constrained set of driver genes and that the driver mutations that most commonly occur in a given cancer also tend to occur the earliest (Gerstung et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gerstung et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The mutation rate of KRAS and TP53 genes in tumors far exceeds those of other genes, suggesting positive selection during tumor evolution.
claims.source: The prominent role of KRAS and TP53 genes in initiating carcinogenesis has been evident from the observation that their mutation rate in tumors far exceeds those of other genes, suggesting that their mutations are subject to positive selection during tumor evolution.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on observed mutation rates mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Background mutation rates differ significantly as a consequence of intrinsic characteristics of DNA sequence and chromatin structure.
claims.source: Unfortunately, methods based on mutation frequency alone cannot reliably indicate which genes are cancer drivers because the background mutation rates differ significantly as a consequence of intrinsic characteristics of DNA sequence and chromatin structure (Michaelson et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Michaelson et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Genes enriched in intrinsic mutation hotspots may accumulate mutations at a significantly higher rate than other genes, creating the illusion of positive selection.
claims.source: Genes enriched in intrinsic mutation hotspots may accumulate mutations at a significantly higher rate than other genes, creating the illusion of positive selection; based on recurrent mutations they may be mistakenly identified as cancer driver genes (Carter, 2019; Buisson et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Carter, 2019 and Buisson et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Chromatin organization has a major influence on regional mutation rates in human cancer cells.
claims.source: Chromatin organization also has a major influence on regional mutation rates in human cancer cells (Schuster-Böckler and Lehner, 2012; Gonzalez-Perez et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schuster-Böckler and Lehner, 2012 and Gonzalez-Perez et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Rates of somatic mutagenesis of genes in cancer are highly cell-type-specific due to cell-of-origin chromatin organization.
claims.source: Moreover, since the cell-of-origin chromatin organization shapes the mutational landscape, rates of somatic mutagenesis of genes in cancer are highly cell-type-specific (Polak et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Polak et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Regional mutation density of passenger mutations across human chromosomes correlates with the cell type the tumor originated from.
claims.source: Actually, since regional mutation density of 'passenger' mutations across the human chromosomes correlates with the cell type the tumor had originated from, this feature may be used to classify human tumors (Salvadores et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Salvadores et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Lawrence et al. identified 224 genes that are significantly mutated in one or more tumor types.
claims.source: They have concluded that 224 genes are significantly mutated in one or more tumor types.
claims.evidence: This refers to the conclusions of Lawrence et al., 2014 study mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Youn and Simon identified 28 genes as driver genes using the ratio of non-silent to silent mutation rates.
claims.source: The authors have identified 28 genes as driver genes, the majority of the significant matches (e.g. EGFR, CDKN2A, KRAS, STK11, TP53, NF1, RB1 PTEN, and NRAS), were well-characterized OGs or TSGs known from earlier studies.
claims.evidence: This refers to the findings of Youn and Simon, 2011 mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Zhou et al. identified 365 genes with significantly increased ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous substitution rate, suggesting positive selection.
claims.source: In a more recent study, Zhou et al., 2017 have identified 365 genes for which the ratio of the nonsynonymous to synonymous substitution rate was significantly increased, suggesting that they are subject to the positive selection of driver mutations.
claims.evidence: This refers to the findings of Zhou et al., 2017 mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Some synonymous mutations may have a significant impact on splicing, RNA stability, RNA folding and translation.
claims.source: This is not necessarily true: some synonymous mutations may have a significant impact on splicing, RNA stability, RNA folding and translation of the transcript of the affected gene and may thus actually act as driver mutations (Supek et al., 2014; Hurst and Batada, 2017; Sharma et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Supek et al., 2014, Hurst and Batada, 2017, and Sharma et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Vogelstein et al. identified 125 genes as Mut-driver genes, of which 71 are TSGs and 54 are OGs.
claims.source: Based on these analyses, the authors have concluded that out of the 20,000 human protein-coding genes, only 125 genes qualify as Mut-driver genes, of these, 71 are TSGs and 54 are OGs (Vogelstein et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This refers to the conclusions of Vogelstein et al., 2013 mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Tamborero et al. identified 291 high-confidence cancer driver genes using five complementary methods.
claims.source: In search of additional driver genes, Tamborero et al., 2013 employed five complementary methods to find genes showing signals of positive selection and identified a list of 291 'high-confidence cancer driver genes' acting on 3205 tumors from 12 different cancer types.
claims.evidence: This refers to the findings of Tamborero et al., 2013 mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Bailey et al. identified 299 driver genes showing signs of positive selection using 26 computational tools.
claims.source: Based on their PanCancer and PanSoftware analysis spanning 9423 tumor exomes, comprising all 33 of The Cancer Genome Atlas projects and using 26 computational tools they have identified 299 driver genes showing signs of positive selection.
claims.evidence: This refers to the findings of Bailey et al., 2018 mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Zhao et al. identified 255 known driver genes and 170 putatively novel driver genes using driverMAPS.
claims.source: The authors have identified 255 known driver genes as well as 170 putatively novel driver genes.
claims.evidence: This refers to the findings of Zhao et al., 2019a mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The Cancer Gene Census describes 719 cancer-driving genes, encompassing 574 Tier 1 genes and 145 Tier 2 genes.
claims.source: CGC describes in detail the effect of a total of 719 cancer-driving genes, encompassing Tier 1 genes (574 genes) and a list of Tier 2 genes (145 genes) from more recent cancer studies that show less detailed indications of a role in cancer.
claims.evidence: This refers to information from the Cancer Gene Census database mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: In around 5% of cancer cases, no driver mutations were identified in tumors.
claims.source: It is noteworthy, however, that, although on average, cancer genomes were shown to contain four to five driver mutations, in around 5% of cases no drivers were identified in tumors (Campbell et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Campbell et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The majority of genomics-based methods were biased as they focused on identifying mutated driver genes positively selected during oncogenesis.
claims.source: We must point out, however, that the majority of genomics-based methods were biased as they defined the aim of cancer genomics as the identification of mutated driver genes (equating them with 'cancer genes') that are causally implicated in oncogenesis (Futreal et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is a critical observation made by the authors about previous methodological approaches.

claims.claim: Most studies neglected the possibility that negative selection may play a significant role in tumor evolution.
claims.source: An inevitable consequence of this focus on positive selection was that most studies neglected the possibility that negative selection may also play a significant role in tumor evolution.
claims.evidence: This is a critical observation made by the authors about previous research approaches.

claims.claim: Proto-oncogenes are expected to show signs of both positive selection for activating mutations and negative selection for inactivating mutations.
claims.source: Proto-oncogenes, however, are expected to show signs of both positive selection for activating mutations and negative selection for inactivating, 'cancer blocking' mutations as their activity is essential for their oncogenic role.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical prediction made by the authors based on the functional requirements of proto-oncogenes.

claims.claim: Zhou et al. identified 923 genes with nonsynonymous to synonymous substitution rate values significantly less than one, reflecting the dominance of negative selection.
claims.source: Conversely, 923 genes had nonsynonymous to synonymous substitution rate values significantly less than one (reflecting the dominance of negative selection), leading the authors to suggest that these negatively selected genes may be important for the growth and survival of cancer cells.
claims.evidence: This refers to the findings of Zhou et al., 2017 mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Pyatnitskiy et al. identified 91 protein-coding genes with amino acid sequences under negative selection.
claims.source: Pyatnitskiy et al., 2015 have also used the dN/dS ratio (the ratio of nonsynonymous and synonymous substitution rates) as an indicator of selective pressure and have identified 91 protein-coding genes ('essential cancer proteins') with amino acid sequences under negative selection.
claims.evidence: This refers to the findings of Pyatnitskiy et al., 2015 mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Weghorn and Sunyaev identified 147 genes with significant negative selection in pan-cancer analysis.
claims.source: Based on pergene estimates of negative selection inferred from the pan-cancer analysis the authors have identified 147 genes with significant negative selection.
claims.evidence: This refers to the findings of Weghorn and Sunyaev, 2017 mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Among the 13 genes showing the strongest signs of negative selection identified by Weghorn and Sunyaev, several are known to promote carcinogenesis.
claims.source: The authors have noted that among the 13 genes showing the strongest signs of negative selection there are several genes (ATAT1, BCL2, CLIP1, GALNT6, CKAP5, and REV1) that are known to promote carcinogenesis.
claims.evidence: This refers to observations made by Weghorn and Sunyaev, 2017 mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Martincorena et al. identified 179 cancer genes under positive selection using a nonsynonymous-to-synonymous substitution rate value >1.
claims.source: Using a nonsynonymous-to-synonymous substitution rate value >1 as a marker of cancer genes under positive selection, they have identified 179 cancer genes, with about 50% of the coding driver mutations being found to occur in novel cancer genes.
claims.evidence: This refers to the findings of Martincorena et al., 2017 mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Martincorena et al. concluded that purifying selection is practically absent in tumors since nearly all coding mutations are tolerated.
claims.source: The authors, however, have concluded that purifying selection is practically absent in tumors since nearly all (>99%) coding mutations are tolerated and escape negative selection.
claims.evidence: This refers to the conclusions of Martincorena et al., 2017 mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The absence of negative selection on coding point mutations in cancer indicates that the vast majority of genes are dispensable for any given somatic lineage.
claims.source: The authors have suggested that this remarkable absence of negative selection on coding point mutations in cancer indicates that the vast majority of genes are dispensable for any given somatic lineage, presumably reflecting the buffering effect of diploidy and the inherent resilience and redundancy built into most cellular pathways.
claims.evidence: This refers to the interpretation by Martincorena et al., 2017 mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Zapata et al. detected significant negative selection in 25 genes.
claims.source: Although Zapata et al., 2018 have also used the ratio of nonsynonymous-to-synonymous substitutions to identify genes that are under selection, they have detected significant negative selection in the case of 25 genes.
claims.evidence: This refers to the findings of Zapata et al., 2018 mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: López et al. showed that purifying selection of essential genes is significant in early phases of tumor evolution before whole genome duplications.
claims.source: López et al., 2020, focusing on dN/dS values for truncating mutations, have shown that purifying selection of essential genes is significant in early phases of tumor evolution (before whole genome duplications), whereas whole-genome doubling allows the accumulation of deleterious alterations.
claims.evidence: This refers to the findings of López et al., 2020 mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Tilk et al. showed that appreciable negative selection is present in tumors with low mutational burden.
claims.source: Tilk et al., 2020 have shown that appreciable negative selection (dN/dS ~ 0.4) is present in tumors with a low mutational burden, while the majority of tumors exhibit dN/dS ratios approaching 1, suggesting that tumors with higher mutational burden do not remove deleterious mutations.
claims.evidence: This refers to the findings of Tilk et al., 2020 mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Van den Eynden and Larsson showed that low dN/dS values observed in malignant melanoma may be due to the predominance of C to T mutations.
claims.source: For example, the authors have shown that the low dN/dS values observed in malignant melanoma may be due to the predominance of C to T mutations in this tumor and do not necessarily indicate gene essentiality.
claims.evidence: This refers to the findings of Van den Eynden and Larsson, 2017 mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Purifying selection is very limited and similar in all tumor types if the dN/dS metric uses mutational signature-derived substitution probabilities.
claims.source: The authors have also shown that purifying selection is very limited and similar in all tumor types if the dN/dS metric uses mutational signature-derived substitution probabilities.
claims.evidence: This refers to the findings of Van den Eynden and Larsson, 2017 mentioned in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The majority of human genes are passenger genes that do not show detectable signals of selection.
claims.source: In harmony with earlier observations, our analyses have confirmed that the vast majority of human genes are PGs that do not show detectable signals of selection, whereas known TSGs are positively selected for inactivating (primarily nonsense and frame-shift) mutations.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' analyses presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Known tumor suppressor genes are positively selected for inactivating (primarily nonsense and frame-shift) mutations.
claims.source: In harmony with earlier observations, our analyses have confirmed that the vast majority of human genes are PGs that do not show detectable signals of selection, whereas known TSGs are positively selected for inactivating (primarily nonsense and frame-shift) mutations.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' analyses presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The approach used in this study correctly assigned known tumor suppressor genes and oncogenes to their respective clusters.
claims.source: The assumption that the cancer genes assigned to these three clusters play significant roles in carcinogenesis has strong support in the case of the first two categories: the approach used in the present study correctly assigned the known, 'gold standard' TSGs and OGs (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is a validation of the authors' method based on known cancer genes.

claims.claim: BMPR2, BRD7, ING1, MGA, PRRT2, RASA1, RNF128, SLC16A1, SPRED1, TGIF1, TNRC6B, ZC3H13, ZFP36L2, and ZNF750 play roles in carcinogenesis as tumor suppressors.
claims.source: Annotation of the majority of these genes (BMPR2, BRD7, ING1, MGA, PRRT2, RASA1, RNF128, SLC16A1, SPRED1, TGIF1, TNRC6B, ZC3H13, ZFP36L2, and ZNF750) has provided convincing evidence for their role in carcinogenesis as tumor suppressors.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' annotation analyses of candidate genes.

claims.claim: TTK is a proto-oncogene that may be converted to an oncogene by truncating mutations affecting the very C-terminal end of the protein.
claims.source: Interestingly, experimental evidence suggests that TTK, encoding dual specificity protein kinase TTK, is a proto-oncogene that may be converted to an OG by truncating mutations affecting the very C-terminal end of the protein, downstream of its kinase domain (for further details see Appendix 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental evidence cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: AURKA, CDK8, IDH3B, MARCH7, RIT1, YAP1, and YES1 play important roles in carcinogenesis as oncogenes.
claims.source: Annotation of these genes has confirmed that they play important roles in carcinogenesis as OGs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' annotation analyses of candidate genes.

claims.claim: CX3CR1, FOXG1, G6PD, MAPK13, NOVA1, PNCK, SLC16A3, SLC2A1, SLC2A8, TBXA2R, TP73, and TRIB2 play important roles in carcinogenesis.
claims.source: Annotations of the genes CX3CR1, FOXG1, G6PD, MAPK13, NOVA1, PNCK, SLC16A3, SLC2A1, SLC2A8, TBXA2R, TP73, and TRIB2 have confirmed that all of them play important roles in carcinogenesis (see Appendix 1) permitting their assignment to various cellular processes of cancer hallmarks (Table 1.).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the authors' annotation analyses of candidate genes.

claims.claim: Negatively selected tumor essential genes fulfill pro-oncogenic functions by promoting cell proliferation, evasion of cell death, replicative immortality, reprogramming of energy metabolism, inducing tumor promoting inflammation, and invasion and metastasis.
claims.source: As discussed below (and in Appendix 1), they fulfill pro-oncogenic functions by promoting cell proliferation (FOXG1, MAPK13, PNCK, TRIB2), evasion of cell death (MAPK13, PNCK, TP73), replicative immortality (NOVA1), reprogramming of energy metabolism of cancer cells (G6PD, SLC16A3, SLC2A1, SLC2A8), inducing tumor promoting inflammation (CX3CR1, MAPK13) and invasion and metastasis (CX3CR1, TBXA2R).
claims.evidence: This is based on functional annotations of the identified genes.

claims.claim: There is a very weak positive correlation between rSMN (a measure of purifying selection) and cell-essentiality scores of transcripts.
claims.source: These analyses have shown that there is a very weak, positive correlation (Pearson's r = 0.05345, p<0.05) between rSMN (a measure of purifying selection) and the cell-essentiality scores of transcripts (Figure 8, Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the authors' analyses shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: Cell essentiality does not contribute significantly to purifying selection during tumor evolution.
claims.source: Since, by definition, there is a negative correlation between the essentiality of genes and their cell-essentiality scores (De Kegel and Ryan, 2019), our data indicate that cell essentiality does not contribute significantly to purifying selection during tumor evolution.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the weak correlation observed between rSMN and cell-essentiality scores.

claims.claim: The cell essentiality scores of negatively selected genes are not significantly different from those of passenger genes.
claims.source: It is also noteworthy that the cell essentiality scores of negatively selected genes (CG_SO2SD rSMN >0.5) are not significantly different from those of PGs (Figure 8, Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the authors' analyses.

claims.claim: Basic cell-essentiality per se does not explain the purifying selection observed for negatively selected genes.
claims.source: This indicates that basic cell-essentiality per se does not explain the purifying selection observed for this cluster of genes.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of CRISPR scores between negatively selected genes and passenger genes.

claims.claim: Only six of the 1014 broadly essential genes are included in the list of negatively selected genes identified in this study.
claims.source: Only six of the 1014 broadly essential genes are included in our list of negatively selected genes (Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from comparing the authors' list with the broadly essential genes defined by De Kegel and Ryan, 2019.

claims.claim: Cell-essentiality defined by CRISPR scores determined experimentally on cell lines is not relevant for negative selection during tumor evolution in vivo.
claims.source: This observation also suggests that cell-essentiality defined by CRISPR scores determined experimentally on cell lines is not relevant for negative selection during tumor evolution in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of overlap between broadly essential genes and negatively selected genes.

claims.claim: Purifying selection of tumor essential genes has more to do with functions specifically required by tumor cells for growth, survival, and metastasis than with general basic cellular functions.
claims.source: Our analyses of cases of strong purifying selection suggest that it has more to do with a function specifically required by the tumor cell for its growth, survival, and metastasis than with general basic cellular functions (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the functional annotations of negatively selected genes.

claims.claim: Genes showing the strongest signals of negative selection include several plasma membrane receptor proteins that cancer cells utilize to promote migration, invasion, and metastasis.
claims.source: It is noteworthy in this respect, that the genes showing the strongest signals of negative selection include several plasma membrane receptor proteins (e.g. ACKR3, CCR2, CCR5, CX3CR1, TBXA2R) that cancer cells utilize to promote migration, invasion, and metastasis (Appendix 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on functional annotations of the identified negatively selected genes.

claims.claim: ACKR3, CX3CR1, and TBXA2R were not assigned to the essential category in any of the 558 tumor cell lines tested by De Kegel and Ryan.
claims.source: Inspection of the data of De Kegel and Ryan, 2019 shows that ACKR3, CX3CR1, TBXA2R were not assigned to the essential category in any of the 558 tumor cell lines tested.
claims.evidence: This is based on inspection of data from De Kegel and Ryan, 2019.

claims.claim: Tumor cells have an increased demand for nutrients that is met by enhanced cellular entry of nutrients through upregulation of specific transporters.
claims.source: The most likely explanation for the tumor essentiality of transporter protein genes SLC16A3, SLC2A1, and SLC2A8 is that tumor cells have an increased demand for nutrients and this demand is met by enhanced cellular entry of nutrients through upregulation of specific transporters (Ganapathy et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ganapathy et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Cancer cells limit their energy metabolism largely to glycolysis even in the presence of oxygen, a state termed 'aerobic glycolysis'.
claims.source: Otto Warburg was the first to observe an anomalous characteristic of cancer-cell energy metabolism: even in the presence of oxygen, cancer cells limit their energy metabolism largely to glycolysis, leading to a state that has been termed 'aerobic glycolysis' (Warburg, 1956a; Warburg, 1956b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Warburg, 1956a and Warburg, 1956b.

claims.claim: Cancer cells compensate for the lower efficiency of ATP production through glycolysis by upregulating glucose transporters such as GLUT1.
claims.source: Cancer cells are known to compensate for the lower efficiency of ATP production through glycolysis than oxidative phosphorylation by upregulating glucose transporters, such as facilitated glucose transporter member 1, GLUT1 (encoded by the SLC2A1 gene), thus increasing glucose import into the cytoplasm (Jones and Thompson, 2009; DeBerardinis et al., 2008; Hsu and Sabatini, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Jones and Thompson, 2009, DeBerardinis et al., 2008, and Hsu and Sabatini, 2008.

claims.claim: High levels of GLUT1 expression correlate with poor overall survival and are associated with increased malignant potential, invasiveness, and poor prognosis.
claims.source: The key importance of GLUT1 in cancer may be illustrated by the fact that high levels of GLUT1 expression correlates with a poor overall survival and is associated with increased malignant potential, invasiveness, and poor prognosis (Wang et al., 2017a; Deng et al., 2018; de Castro et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2017a, Deng et al., 2018, and de Castro et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Knockdown of GLUT1 inhibits cell glycolysis and proliferation and inhibits the growth of tumors.
claims.source: The tumor essentiality of GLUT1 may also be illustrated by the fact that knockdown of GLUT1 inhibits cell glycolysis and proliferation and inhibits the growth of tumors (Xiao et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xiao et al., 2018.

claims.claim: GLUT1 is a promising target for cancer therapy.
claims.source: In view of its essentiality for tumor growth, GLUT1 is a promising target for cancer therapy (Shibuya et al., 2015; Noguchi et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2017d).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Shibuya et al., 2015, Noguchi et al., 2016, and Chen et al., 2017d.

claims.claim: The YAP1-TEAD1-GLUT1 axis plays a major role in reprogramming of cancer energy metabolism by modulating glycolysis.
claims.source: Recent studies suggest that the YAP1-TEAD1-GLUT1 axis plays a major role in reprogramming of cancer energy metabolism by modulating glycolysis (Lin and Xu, 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lin and Xu, 2017.

claims.claim: GLUT8 is overexpressed in and is required for proliferation and viability of tumors.
claims.source: In harmony with this interpretation, there is evidence that GLUT8 is overexpressed in and is required for proliferation and viability of tumors (Goldman et al., 2006; McBrayer et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Goldman et al., 2006 and McBrayer et al., 2012.

claims.claim: MCT4 efficiently transports L-lactate out of the cell, ensuring survival and maintenance of the glycolytic phenotype of tumor cells.
claims.source: Survival and maintenance of the glycolytic phenotype of tumor cells is ensured by monocarboxylate transporter 4 (MCT4, encoded by the SLC16A3 gene) that efficiently transports L-lactate out of the cell (Ganapathy et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ganapathy et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Knockdown of MCT4 increased tumor-free survival and decreased in vitro proliferation rate of tumor cells.
claims.source: As high metabolic and proliferative rates in cancer cells lead to production of large amounts of lactate, extruding transporters are essential for the survival of cancer cells as illustrated by the fact that knockdown of MCT4 increased tumor-free survival and decreased in vitro proliferation rate of tumor cells (Andersen et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Andersen et al., 2018.

claims.claim: MCT4 depletion reduced the ability of breast cancer cells to grow.
claims.source: Using a functional screen Baenke et al., 2015 have also demonstrated that monocarboxylate transporter four is an important regulator of breast cancer cell survival: MCT4 depletion reduced the ability of breast cancer cells to grow, suggesting that it might be a valuable therapeutic target.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Baenke et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Expression of MCT4 is increased in tumors and correlates with clinical outcome.
claims.source: In harmony with the essentiality of MCT4 for tumor growth, several studies indicate that expression of the hypoxia-inducible monocarboxylate transporter MCT4 is increased in tumors and its expression correlates with clinical outcome, thus it may serve as a valuable prognostic factor (Witkiewicz et al., 2012; Doyen et al., 2014; Baek et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Witkiewicz et al., 2012, Doyen et al., 2014, and Baek et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Selective inhibition of MCT4 to block lactic acid efflux is a promising therapeutic strategy against highly glycolytic malignant tumors.
claims.source: Consistent with the key importance of MCT4 for the survival of tumor cells, its selective inhibition to block lactic acid efflux appears to be a promising therapeutic strategy against highly glycolytic malignant tumors (Choi et al., 2016; Todenhöfer et al., 2018; Choi et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2019b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Choi et al., 2016, Todenhöfer et al., 2018, Choi et al., 2018, and Zhao et al., 2019b.

claims.claim: ACKR3 is a well-known oncogene present in Tier 1 of the Cancer Gene Census.
claims.source: Significantly, ACKR3 is a well-known OG, present in Tier 1 of the Cancer Gene Census.
claims.evidence: This is based on information from the Cancer Gene Census database.

claims.claim: ACKR3 plays a key role in tumor invasion and metastasis.
claims.source: Several studies support the key role of ACKR3 in tumor invasion and metastasis (Li et al., 2014; Stacer et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2017; Puddinu et al., 2017; Melo et al., 2018; Qian et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Knock-down or pharmacological inhibition of ACKR3 reduces tumor invasion and metastasis.
claims.source: Since knock-down or pharmacological inhibition of ACKR3 has been shown to reduce tumor invasion and metastasis, ACKR3 is a promising therapeutic target for the control of tumor dissemination (for further details see Appendix 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on studies mentioned in the manuscript and detailed in Appendix 1.

claims.claim: The proportion of silent substitutions is significantly higher for germline mutations than for somatic mutations of tumors.
claims.source: Comparison of the patterns of germline and somatic mutations of human transcripts (Supplementary file 7) has revealed that the proportion of silent substitutions is significantly higher for germline mutations than for somatic mutations of tumors (fSg: 0.33900 versus fSs: 0.24604, p<0.05).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the authors' comparative analyses.

claims.claim: The proportions of nonsense and missense mutations are significantly lower for germline mutations than for somatic mutations of tumors.
claims.source: Conversely, the proportions of nonsense and missense mutations are significantly lower for germline mutations than for somatic mutations of tumors (fNg: 0.02329 versus fNs: 0.04669, p<0.05; fMg: 0.63771 versus fMs: 0.70727, p<0.05).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the authors' comparative analyses.

claims.claim: The pattern of distribution of transcripts in 3D scatter plots of fM, fN, and fS parameters for germline mutations is strikingly different from that of somatic mutations in cancer.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 9, the pattern of the distribution of transcripts in 3D scatter plots of fM, fN, and fS parameters for germline mutations are strikingly different from those observed in the case of fM, fN, and fS parameters of somatic mutations in cancer (compare Figure 9A and B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 9 comparing germline and somatic mutation patterns.

claims.claim: There is only weak correlation between the strength of purifying selection of genes during tumor evolution and organismal evolution.
claims.source: Comparison of the fS, rSM, and rSMN parameters of germline and somatic mutations of transcripts (Figure 10, Supplementary file 7) has shown that there is only weak correlation between the strength of purifying selection of genes during tumor evolution and organismal evolution.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the authors' comparative analyses shown in Figure 10.

claims.claim: Candidate tumor essential genes display significantly stronger signals of purifying selection during tumor evolution than during organismal evolution relative to other genes.
claims.source: These comparisons have also revealed that – relative to other genes – the candidate TEGs identified in the present study (CG_SO2SD_rSMN >0.5) display significantly stronger signals of purifying selection during tumor evolution than during organismal evolution (Figure 10, Supplementary file 7).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the authors' comparative analyses shown in Figure 10.

claims.claim: The negative selection of candidate tumor essential genes during tumor evolution is not a simple reflection of their essentiality at the organism level.
claims.source: These observations indicate that the negative selection of candidate TEGs during tumor evolution is not a simple reflection of their essentiality at the organism level; it is more likely that they serve tumor-specific functions.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of selection patterns in tumor versus organismal evolution.

claims.claim: There is a very weak negative correlation between the strength of purifying selection of transcripts (rSMNg) and their cell-essentiality scores.
claims.source: These analyses have shown that there is a very weak negative correlation (Pearson's r = −0.03662, p<0.05) between the strength of purifying selection of transcripts (rSMNg) and their cell-essentiality scores (Figure 11, Supplementary file 7).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from the authors' analyses shown in Figure 11.

claims.claim: Essentiality of cell-level functions measured by cell-essentiality scores contribute to, but do not explain the strength of purifying selection observed during organismal evolution.
claims.source: This observation also indicates that essentiality of cell-level functions measured by cell-essentiality scores contribute to, but do not explain the strength of purifying selection observed during organismal evolution.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the weak negative correlation between rSMNg and cell-essentiality scores.

claims.claim: The PCAWG driver list identifies a total of 722 protein-coding genes as cancer driver genes and 22 non-coding driver mutations.
claims.source: As a result of combined efforts, the PCAWG driver list identifies a total of 722 protein-coding genes as cancer driver genes and 22 non-coding driver mutations (Rheinbay et al., 2020; Campbell et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is based on citations to Rheinbay et al., 2020 and Campbell et al., 2020.

claims.claim: The core mission of cancer-genome sequencing projects to provide a catalogue of driver mutations has been achieved according to Nature editorial.
claims.source: In a recent editorial, commenting on a suite of papers on the genetic causes of cancer, Nature has expressed the view that the core of the mission of cancer-genome sequencing projects—to provide a catalogue of driver mutations that could give rise to cancer—has been achieved (Editorial, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is based on a citation to an editorial in Nature.

claims.claim: The observation that 5% of tumors lack known drivers suggests that cancer driver discovery is not yet complete.
claims.source: As pointed out by the authors, this observation suggests that cancer driver discovery is not yet complete, possibly due to failure of the available bioinformatic algorithms.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation by Campbell et al., 2020 cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: About half of cancer driver genes remain unknown based on the fraction of tumors lacking known drivers.
claims.source: Assuming that tumors, on average, must have driver mutations affecting at least four or five cancer genes and that known and unknown cancer genes play similar roles in carcinogenesis, the observation that a 0.05 fraction of tumors has no known drivers (i.e. they are driven by four to five unknown cancer drivers) indicates that about half of the drivers is still unknown.
claims.evidence: This is a calculation and inference made by the authors based on the data from Campbell et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Hundreds of cancer driver genes remain to be identified based on the estimated fraction of unknown drivers.
claims.source: Since the list of known drivers used in the study of the ICGC/TCGA Pan-Cancer Analysis of Whole Genomes Consortium (Campbell et al., 2020) comprises 722 driver genes, these observations suggest that hundreds of cancer driver genes remain to be identified.
claims.evidence: This is an inference made by the authors based on their calculations.

claims.claim: The approach reported in this study will promote the identification of numerous novel oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, and pro-oncogenic tumor essential genes that may serve as therapeutic targets.
claims.source: We believe that the approach reported here will promote the identification of numerous novel OGs, TSGs, and pro-oncogenic TEGs that may serve as therapeutic targets.
claims.evidence: This is a concluding statement by the authors about the potential impact of their work.

claims.claim: The majority of human genes form a central cluster characterized by fS, fM, and fN values close to those expected assuming no mutation bias and absence of selection.
claims.source: Our analyses have shown that in 3D scatter plots of the fS, fM, and fN values of transcripts the majority of genes are present in a central cluster characterized by fS, fM, and fN values close to those expected assuming no mutation bias and absence of selection, consistent with the view that they correspond to PGs (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analyses shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Known oncogenes have a significantly larger fraction of nonsynonymous substitutions than passenger genes.
claims.source: It is noteworthy that these driver genes separate significantly from the central cluster and from each other: OGs have a significantly larger fraction of nonsynonymous, whereas TSGs have significantly larger fraction of nonsense substitutions.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and supported by statistical analyses.

claims.claim: Known tumor suppressor genes have a significantly larger fraction of nonsense substitutions than passenger genes.
claims.source: It is noteworthy that these driver genes separate significantly from the central cluster and from each other: OGs have a significantly larger fraction of nonsynonymous, whereas TSGs have significantly larger fraction of nonsense substitutions.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and supported by statistical analyses.

claims.claim: A fourth cluster of genes deviates from the clusters of passenger genes, oncogenes, and tumor suppressor genes, showing high fS, rSM, and rSMN values suggesting purifying selection.
claims.source: There is, however, a fourth cluster of genes that deviates from the clusters of PGs, OGs, and TSGs (Figures 2, 3 and 4). The high fS, rSM, and rSMN values of the transcripts in this group suggest that they are subject to purifying selection during tumor evolution, raising the possibility that this group may contain genes essential for the survival of tumors.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figures 2, 3, and 4 and interpreted by the authors.

claims.claim: The separation of clusters of passenger genes, oncogenes, tumor suppressor genes, and tumor essential genes is relatively insensitive to transcript-specific differences in mutation probabilities.
claims.source: As shown in Figures 5, 6 and 7, the distribution of transcripts in these 3D scatter plots are similar to those observed in the corresponding Figures 2, 3 and 4, indicating that the separation of the clusters of PGs, OGs, TSGs, and TEGs is relatively insensitive to transcript-specific differences in mutation probabilities.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing Figures 2-4 with Figures 5-7.

results.result: Tumor suppressor genes are positively selected for inactivating mutations (primarily nonsense and frameshift mutations) during tumor evolution, as demonstrated by significantly higher fractions of nonsense substitutions compared to passenger genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C65, and C113 collectively demonstrate that TSGs show positive selection for inactivating mutations. The 3D scatter plot analyses (Figures 2-4) show TSGs separating from passenger genes with significantly higher fN values and rNSM ratios, providing strong statistical and visual evidence. The method correctly assigns known 'gold standard' TSGs (C66), validating the approach.

results.result: Oncogenes display dual selection patterns: positive selection for activating missense mutations and negative selection for inactivating nonsense mutations, reflecting their requirement for functional activity in carcinogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C51, and C112 are supported by data showing oncogenes have significantly higher fractions of missense mutations (fM) and lower fractions of nonsense mutations compared to passenger genes (Figures 2-4). The theoretical prediction (C51) is validated by empirical observations, and the method correctly assigns known oncogenes (C66).

results.result: A fourth cluster of genes shows strong negative selection during tumor evolution, characterized by high synonymous-to-nonsynonymous mutation ratios (high fS, rSM, rSMN values), suggesting these genes are essential for tumor cell growth and survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, and C114 identify a novel cluster of negatively selected genes distinct from passenger genes, oncogenes, and TSGs (Figures 2-4). The high rSMN values indicate purifying selection. Functional validation of representative genes (C70, C71) confirms their pro-oncogenic roles in cancer hallmarks, supporting the interpretation of tumor essentiality.

results.result: Fourteen novel candidate tumor suppressor genes (BMPR2, BRD7, ING1, MGA, PRRT2, RASA1, RNF128, SLC16A1, SPRED1, TGIF1, TNRC6B, ZC3H13, ZFP36L2, ZNF750) were identified and validated through functional annotation.
results.evaluation: Claim C67 is supported by the selection of genes from the positively selected cluster (high rNSM values) and subsequent literature-based functional validation showing their tumor suppressor roles. The genes were selected using stringent criteria and show mutation patterns consistent with TSGs.

results.result: Seven novel candidate oncogenes (AURKA, CDK8, IDH3B, MARCH7, RIT1, YAP1, YES1) were identified and validated through functional annotation.
results.evaluation: Claim C69 is supported by selection from the cluster showing positive selection for missense mutations and negative selection for nonsense mutations (high rMSN, low rNSM values), with subsequent functional validation confirming oncogenic roles. The approach successfully identifies both known and novel oncogenes.

results.result: Twelve negatively selected tumor essential genes (CX3CR1, FOXG1, G6PD, MAPK13, NOVA1, PNCK, SLC16A3, SLC2A1, SLC2A8, TBXA2R, TP73, TRIB2) fulfill tumor-specific pro-oncogenic functions including metabolic reprogramming, invasion, and metastasis, rather than basic cellular functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C70, C71, C78, and C79 are supported by functional annotations showing these genes play specific roles in cancer hallmarks (Table 1). The genes show high rSMN values indicating negative selection. Detailed mechanistic evidence is provided for metabolic genes (SLC2A1, SLC16A3) and invasion/metastasis genes (CX3CR1, TBXA2R), supporting tumor-specific essentiality.

results.result: Cell essentiality (measured by CRISPR scores) does not significantly contribute to purifying selection during tumor evolution, as evidenced by weak correlation (r=0.05345) between rSMN and cell-essentiality scores and minimal overlap with broadly essential genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C77 are supported by statistical analyses (Figure 8) showing very weak positive correlation between purifying selection strength and cell-essentiality scores. Only 6 of 1014 broadly essential genes overlap with negatively selected genes (C76), and CRISPR scores of negatively selected genes are not significantly different from passenger genes (C74), strongly supporting the conclusion.

results.result: GLUT1 (SLC2A1) is a tumor essential gene under negative selection that is critical for the Warburg effect in cancer cells, with high expression correlating with poor prognosis and knockdown inhibiting tumor growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C86 provide convergent evidence from multiple studies showing GLUT1's essentiality for tumor metabolism. The gene shows negative selection (high rSMN), and extensive literature citations support its role in aerobic glycolysis (C82, C83), clinical correlations (C84), functional validation (C85), and therapeutic potential (C86).

results.result: MCT4 (SLC16A3) is a tumor essential gene under negative selection that is critical for lactate efflux in glycolytic tumor cells, with expression correlating with clinical outcome and knockdown reducing tumor growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C93 provide strong evidence for MCT4's tumor essentiality through its role in maintaining glycolytic phenotype (C89), functional validation showing knockdown effects (C90, C91), clinical correlations (C92), and therapeutic potential (C93). Multiple independent studies support these conclusions.

results.result: ACKR3 is a well-characterized oncogene that shows negative selection and plays a key role in tumor invasion and metastasis, with knockdown or inhibition reducing metastatic spread.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C96 are supported by ACKR3's presence in Cancer Gene Census Tier 1 (C94), multiple studies demonstrating its role in invasion/metastasis (C95), and functional validation of therapeutic targeting (C96). This exemplifies how some oncogenes show predominantly negative selection patterns.

results.result: Selection patterns differ significantly between tumor evolution and organismal evolution: germline mutations show stronger purifying selection overall, while candidate tumor essential genes show significantly stronger negative selection during tumor evolution than organismal evolution, indicating tumor-specific functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C102 are supported by comparative statistical analyses (Figures 9-10) showing significant differences in mutation patterns between germline and somatic contexts. The weak correlation (Pearson's r values 0.02635-0.1127) between selection strengths in the two contexts (C100) and the differential selection of TEGs (C101) strongly support tumor-specific essentiality (C102).

results.result: The separation of gene clusters (passenger genes, oncogenes, tumor suppressors, tumor essential genes) is relatively insensitive to transcript-specific differences in mutation probabilities.
results.evaluation: Claim C115 is supported by comparison of analyses using observed values (Figures 2-4) versus expected values corrected for mutational signatures (Figures 5-7), showing similar cluster patterns. This demonstrates the robustness of the clustering approach and validates that selection signals are not artifacts of mutation bias.

results.result: The clustering approach correctly assigns known 'gold standard' tumor suppressor genes and oncogenes to their respective clusters, validating the methodology.
results.evaluation: Claim C66 is supported by successful assignment of known TSGs and OGs from Vogelstein et al. 2013 to appropriate clusters based on mutation patterns. This validation against established cancer genes provides strong support for the method's ability to identify novel cancer genes.

results.result: Approximately 5% of tumors lack known driver mutations, and based on the assumption that tumors require 4-5 driver mutations, this suggests about half of cancer driver genes (hundreds of genes) remain to be identified.
results.evaluation: Claims C48, C107, C108, and C109 involve a calculation based on the assumption that known and unknown cancer genes play similar roles (C108). While C48 is supported by citation to Campbell et al. 2020, the inference that half of drivers remain unknown (C108) relies on assumptions about driver mutation requirements and equal detectability that may not hold. The calculation is logical but speculative.

results.result: Previous genomics-based methods were biased toward identifying positively selected driver genes and neglected the role of negative selection in tumor evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C49 and C50 are supported by the authors' critical review of prior literature showing most studies focused on positive selection. The identification of numerous negatively selected genes in the current study that were missed by previous approaches validates this criticism. However, this is primarily a methodological observation rather than a novel biological finding.

results.result: Martincorena et al. concluded that purifying selection is practically absent in tumors because nearly all coding mutations are tolerated, suggesting most genes are dispensable due to diploidy and pathway redundancy.
results.evaluation: Claims C57 and C58 accurately report the conclusions of Martincorena et al. 2017 as cited. However, the current manuscript's data contradict these conclusions, showing significant negative selection. This represents accurate reporting of prior work that the authors challenge with their own findings.

results.result: There is a very weak negative correlation (r=-0.03662) between purifying selection strength during organismal evolution (rSMNg) and cell-essentiality scores, indicating cell-level essentiality contributes to but does not fully explain purifying selection during organismal evolution.
results.evaluation: Claims C103 and C104 are supported by statistical analysis (Figure 11) showing weak negative correlation. This finding parallels the tumor evolution results, suggesting that essentiality measured by CRISPR screens captures only part of the selective pressures operating at the organismal level.

results.result: The majority of human genes form a central cluster with mutation parameters (fS, fM, fN) close to neutral expectations, consistent with passenger gene status.
results.evaluation: Claim C111 is supported by 3D scatter plot analyses (Figure 2) showing most genes cluster around expected neutral values. This establishes the baseline against which cancer genes are identified and validates the assumption that most genes do not play significant roles in carcinogenesis.

results.result: TTK is a proto-oncogene that may be converted to an oncogene by truncating mutations affecting the C-terminal end downstream of its kinase domain.
results.evaluation: Claim C68 is supported by experimental evidence cited in the manuscript and detailed in Appendix 1. This represents an interesting exception where truncating mutations can activate rather than inactivate a proto-oncogene, though the mechanism is not fully detailed in the main text.

results.result: The approach reported in this study will promote identification of numerous novel oncogenes, tumor suppressors, and tumor essential genes that may serve as therapeutic targets.
results.evaluation: Claim C110 is a forward-looking statement supported by the successful identification and validation of multiple novel cancer genes in the current study. The identification of negatively selected tumor essential genes represents a particularly promising avenue for therapeutic targeting, as demonstrated by the GLUT1 and MCT4 examples.
